A social worker who has spent significant time with him said Malvo frequently creates self-portraits in which a tear is shown running down his face.

Malvo, now 22, is serving a life sentence at Red Onion, Virginia’s most secure prison, a maximum-security facility located near the Kentucky border. He is confined to his cell for 23 hours each day.

Carmeta Albarus-Lindo, the social worker who has worked with Malvo for hundreds of hours since his arrest and conviction, said he is no longer the same person he was when he and John Allen Muhammad frightened the Washington region during a 23-day shooting spree five years ago this month that killed 10 people.

“The most I can do is to continue to be there, because that is his greatest fear — that, you know, another parental figure would abandon him because that was what he’d been exposed to all his life,” Albarus-Lindo said.

She said Muhammad became one of those parental figures. He met Malvo in the Caribbean almost two years before the 2002 attacks began and later took on the role of a substitute father to the teenager, according to Albarus-Lindo. She said Muhammad persuaded Malvo that violence was the only means of addressing what they saw as injustices against African-Americans.

Albarus-Lindo said Muhammad told Malvo when to sleep each night and made him memorize sections of “The Art of War,” the ancient Chinese military strategy text. In her view, Malvo was “brainwashed” into helping Muhammad carry out the killings.

Prosecutors, however, have argued that Malvo understood his actions, even though he was 17 at the time.

“When I first met him, I thought he was coldblooded,” said Paul Ebert, the commonwealth’s attorney for Prince William County, Virginia. “He was a person who had chosen a life of crime.”

Some investigators said they were deeply upset when a Virginia jury decided not to sentence Malvo to death.

“That was the hardest day of my career,” said April Carroll of the Bureau of Alcohol, Firearms and Tobacco. “I felt that day we had failed when Malvo was not sentenced to death.”

Other people, including some relatives of victims, said they accepted the jury’s decision. Vicki Buchanan Snyder, whose brother James “Sonny” Buchanan was shot in the back while cutting grass at a Maryland car dealership, said she was “satisfied” with the verdict.

Albarus-Lindo said Malvo will “never forgive himself for what has happened.” She recalled that when she first started meeting with him, he still referred to Muhammad as “Dad.” According to her, it took months before he stopped doing so. During that period, she said, Malvo enrolled in college correspondence courses and started drawing.

Muhammad is incarcerated at Sussex One, a Virginia prison. In a DVD recorded inside the prison last year and obtained exclusively by CNN, he said he is “still fighting” while on death row. He said he wanted to “correct” what he described as “inaccurate statements” made by the media about his relationship with Malvo, though he did not explain specifically what he meant.

Muhammad’s former wife, Mildred, said she believes she had been the snipers’ true intended target from the start. She lives with her children in the Washington suburbs and operates Afterthetrauma.org, a Web site focused on victims of domestic abuse.

Mildred Muhammad said she thinks her ex-husband wanted to kill her in retaliation because she had obtained custody of their three children. Regarding his connection to Malvo, she said she also believes John Allen Muhammad manipulated and brainwashed the younger man.

“That boy was a victim before he even knew it,” she said. “His life was over when he said, ‘Hi.’”

At the same time, prosecutors and many victims’ families have emphasized that Malvo was not merely a passive victim of Muhammad’s control. Ultimately, Malvo’s case forces a broader question: how should society judge a person who committed horrific crimes as a teenager under the influence of a manipulative adult, but who later appears to have changed? For victims’ relatives, Malvo’s remorse brings mixed reactions. She has described Lee Malvo as a boy drawn into Muhammad’s orbit, but has also stressed the lasting trauma inflicted on the victims, their families and the communities targeted.

Behind prison walls, Malvo’s future is narrow: no parole, no release date, no return to the life he had before the shootings. Those who have spoken with him say he spends time reading, reflecting and trying to understand how he became part of one of the nation’s most notorious killing sprees.

But for the families of those killed — and for the survivors who still carry physical and emotional wounds — the fifth anniversary is not about Malvo’s introspection. **After the Beltway sniper attacks, two lives behind bars — and a debate over blame**

**By Staff Writer**  
**Dateline: Washington**

Years after the terror of the 2002 Beltway sniper attacks faded from the daily routines of the Washington region, the aftermath continued in courtrooms, prisons and in the memories of families who lost loved ones to random gunfire.

For three weeks in October 2002, residents across Maryland, Virginia and Washington, DC, lived under siege as shootings at gas stations, parking lots and streets left 10 people dead and three others wounded. The attackers — John Allen Muhammad, a Gulf War veteran, and Lee Boyd Malvo, a teenager from Jamaica — were eventually arrested at a Maryland rest stop, asleep in a blue Chevrolet Caprice modified so a shooter could fire from the trunk.

Muhammad was sentenced to death and executed in Virginia in 2009. Malvo, who was 17 at the time of the crimes, received multiple life sentences. But the story did not end with their convictions.

### A young inmate living with old crimes

In prison, Malvo became known not only as one of the most infamous criminals in America, but also as a man haunted by what he had done. Over the years, he gave interviews in which he expressed remorse and described the killings as a source of overwhelming shame.

He also drew.

Some of Malvo’s prison artwork reflected a dark internal world — images tied to violence, guilt and the psychological grip he said Muhammad had over him. The drawings became part of the public portrait of a man who, as a teenager, had participated in crimes that terrified an entire region and devastated families.

Malvo has said he thinks constantly about the victims. In interviews, he has described himself as “a monster” for his role in the shootings and has apologized to the families, though many relatives have said remorse cannot undo the damage.

For them, the facts remain brutally simple: their loved ones were killed at random while doing ordinary things — pumping gas, shopping, walking to school, going about daily life.

### Was Malvo brainwashed?

One of the most debated questions in the years after the attacks has been whether Malvo was brainwashed by Muhammad.

Malvo’s attorneys and some psychologists have argued that Muhammad groomed and indoctrinated him. They portrayed Malvo as a vulnerable teenager who had been abandoned by adults, searching for stability and guidance when Muhammad took control of his life. According to that view, Muhammad isolated Malvo, trained him, fed him a worldview built on violence and obedience, and turned him into a weapon.

Malvo himself has described Muhammad as a father figure who controlled him emotionally and psychologically. He said Muhammad taught him to suppress empathy and to see the shootings as part of a larger mission.

But prosecutors and many victims’ relatives rejected the idea that Malvo was merely a brainwashed child. They argued that he made choices, pulled the trigger in some attacks and participated in planning and evasion. To them, his youth explained some of his vulnerability but did not erase his responsibility.

That divide has shaped much of the public discussion about Malvo: Was he a manipulated teenager, a willing killer, or both?

Courts have also revisited his punishment because he was a juvenile at the time of the crimes. U.S. Supreme Court rulings limiting mandatory life-without-parole sentences for juveniles opened the door to new legal arguments. Still, Malvo remains imprisoned, and the families of victims have repeatedly stressed that the focus should remain on those who were killed and wounded.

### Muhammad’s claims from death row

John Allen Muhammad, meanwhile, maintained from death row that he was innocent or wrongly convicted, even as prosecutors described him as the mastermind of the attacks.

Authorities said Muhammad’s motives included revenge against his ex-wife and a broader plan to create chaos. Investigators and prosecutors argued that the random shootings were meant to mask an intended target and terrorize the region.

Muhammad denied responsibility in various ways and continued to challenge the case against him. He represented himself at times during legal proceedings and rejected the prosecution’s narrative. But courts upheld his convictions and death sentence.

He was executed by lethal injection in Virginia in November 2009.

For many victims’ families, Muhammad’s continued claims only deepened their anger. They viewed him as manipulative and unrepentant. Malvo’s later remorse, while noted, has also been met with skepticism by some who say no apology can balance the lives taken.

### A region changed

The Beltway sniper attacks changed how people in the Washington area moved through the world. Parents feared school drop-offs. Drivers crouched while pumping gas. White vans and box trucks drew suspicion. Police agencies coordinated across jurisdictions under intense public pressure.

The arrests brought relief, but not closure.

The aftermath has been defined by competing narratives: a mastermind who insisted from death row that the story was wrong; a teenage accomplice who later said he was controlled and now lives with shame; and families who continue to carry the permanent cost of a killing spree that turned ordinary public spaces into scenes of terror.

More than two decades later, the central facts remain: 10 people were killed, three were wounded, and an entire region learned how quickly normal life could be shattered.
